\[
W_{j,k}(f) = W_j(|f|)\, V\!\left(K_j\, \frac{f_y}{f_x} - k\right),
\quad
|f_y| \le |f_x|,\ k = -K_j \ldots K_j,
\qquad
c_{j,k} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\big(W_{j,k}\, \mathcal{F} I\big),
\qquad
\hat{I} = \mathcal{F}^{-1}\Big(W_{\text{low}}^2\, \mathcal{F} I + \sum_{j,k} W_{j,k}\, \mathcal{F}\big(\eta(c_{j,k})\big)\Big),
\qquad
4 K_0 = \text{16}
\]

The formula shows the default parameter values.

where

- \(f_x, f_y\): A frequency in cycles per pixel, with f_y growing downward
- \(W_j\): The radial window of band j. Band 0 is the finest.
- \(V\): The slope window, with Meyer's polynomial nu
- \(K_j\): The number of shears on each side of the cone axis in band j
- \(c_{j,k}\): The coefficients of tile j k
- \(\eta\): Hard thresholding at k sigma times the RMS of the mask

Cone-adapted shearlets, after Guo and Labate, split the spectrum into a horizontal cone, where |f_y| <= |f_x|, and a vertical cone. In each cone, the directions are set by shearing. The slope f_y / f_x, or f_x / f_y in the vertical cone, is cut into windows centered at k / K_j. So the directions are evenly spaced in slope, not in angle. Here the radial windows W_j are those of the curvelet-inspired filter, with squares that add up to 1. V uses Meyer's polynomial nu, so the squares of neighboring slope windows add up to 1 too. The tiles of the two cones that meet at a diagonal are joined into one, which gives 4 K_j tiles per band. K_j halves every second scale toward the coarse end. Noise removal and orientation work as in the curvelet-inspired filter. The tiles are not shearlets of a shearlet transform, which come with their own sampling and generating functions, so this is a shearlet-inspired filter.
